motifs.text: Homer's extended similes compare scenes of battle to images drawn from nature and everyday life: lions attacking cattle, storms at sea, forest fires, farmers threshing grain, a mother brushing a fly from her sleeping child. They slow down the action, offer a vision of a world beyond the war, and often express emotions that the characters cannot. Many are drawn from the world of peace, so that war is constantly set against the life it destroys.

motifs.title: Supplication
motifs.text: Supplication (hikesia), the ritual of clasping a person's knees or touching their chin to beg for mercy, appears throughout the poem. Chryses' plea is rejected in Book 1, Thetis' supplication of Zeus succeeds, suppliants on the battlefield are killed by Agamemnon and Akhilleus, and Priam's supplication of Akhilleus in Book 24 is finally granted. The fate of suppliants measures the moral state of the war.

motifs.title: Arming scenes and armour
motifs.text: Before an aristeia, a warrior arms himself in a set sequence: greaves, breastplate, sword, shield, helmet, spear. Such typical scenes are building blocks of oral composition, expanded or compressed as needed. Akhilleus' armour in particular passes from Akhilleus to Patroclus to Hector, marking each wearer for death, until Akhilleus receives the new armour made by Hephaestus.

motifs.title: Funeral rites and lament
motifs.text: Proper burial is essential in the Homeric world, and the threat of leaving a body to dogs and birds is the worst insult. The poem moves from the anonymous dead of the proem to the elaborate funeral of Patroclus and the final funeral of Hector. Laments by women and men articulate the losses of war and give the poem its closing voice.

motifs.title: Gifts, prizes and ransom
motifs.text: The exchange of goods structures social relations in the poem. Prizes measure honour, gifts seal friendships and reconciliations, and ransom allows the return of captives and bodies. The poem begins with a ransom refused (Chryses) and ends with a ransom accepted (Priam), framing the wrath of Akhilleus between two acts of exchange.

symbols.title: The Shield of Akhilleus
symbols.text: The shield made by Hephaestus in Book 18 represents the whole world: the heavens, the earth and the sea, cities at peace and at war, farming, celebration, and the river Ocean around the edge. Carried by Akhilleus into his most violent fighting, it holds within it an image of everything that war threatens. It has also been read as a symbol of the poem itself, a work of art that contains a world [[taplin1980]].

symbols.title: The scales of Zeus
symbols.text: Zeus' golden scales appear at the turning points of Books 8 and 22, weighing the fates of armies and of Hector. They represent the inevitable working of fate and Zeus' will, and the visible moment when a man's destiny is decided.

symbols.title: The sceptre
symbols.text: The staff held by speakers in the assembly and the sceptre of Agamemnon, passed down from Zeus through Hermes and Pelops, symbolise legitimate authority. Akhilleus' oath on the sceptre in Book 1, and his throwing it down, mark his rejection of Agamemnon's authority; Odysseus' use of it to beat Thersites in Book 2 shows its force.

symbols.title: The Achaean wall
symbols.text: Built in Book 7 and broken through in Book 12, the wall around the Achaean ships is destined to be erased by the gods after the war. It symbolises the impermanence of human works and the contrast between physical monuments, which vanish, and the poem, which remains.

debates.title: The Homeric Question
text: The Homeric Question asks who composed the Iliad and the Odyssey, when, how and in what form. Ancient scholars already discussed whether the same poet composed both epics. In 1795 Friedrich August Wolf argued that the poems had been assembled from shorter oral songs, launching a debate between 'analysts', who sought to identify earlier layers and later additions, and 'unitarians', who defended the poem's unity of design.

Today most scholars accept that the Iliad grew out of an oral tradition but disagree about how it became fixed. Some believe that a single poet dictated or wrote a monumental version; others, such as Gregory Nagy, see a gradual crystallisation over centuries of performance. Martin West argued for a single poet working with writing over a long period [[west2011]] [[west2011b]] [[nagy1979]] [[graziosi2002]].

debates.title: Oral-formulaic composition and its critics
text: Milman Parry demonstrated that Homeric epithets and phrases form an economical system of formulas suited to oral composition in performance [[parry1971]]. Albert Lord's fieldwork among South Slavic singers showed how such poets compose long songs without writing [[lord1960]]. The Parry-Lord theory transformed the study of Homer and of oral poetry worldwide.

Critics have questioned whether the theory can explain the Iliad's exceptional length, coherence and artistry. Adam Parry, Milman's son, asked whether formulaic composition left room for individual meaning [[parry1966]]. Others noted that the formulas are often used with subtle point and that the poem displays a design that seems to require a single controlling mind [[kirk1985]] [[edwards1987]].

debates.title: Date and the historical Troy
text: Most scholars date the Iliad between the late eighth and the mid-seventh century BC. The older consensus favoured a date around 750–700 BC; Martin West, pointing to apparent echoes of Hesiod and to allusions that seem to reflect the world of the seventh century, placed it between about 680 and 640 BC [[west2011]]. Linguistic and archaeological arguments have been used on both sides, and the question is bound up with how and when the text was written down.

The excavations at Hisarlık by Heinrich Schliemann and later archaeologists revealed a city destroyed around 1200 BC, and Hittite documents mention a city called Wilusa. Joachim Latacz argued that these finds support the historicity of a Trojan war [[latacz2004]]. Denys Page earlier explored what historical memories might survive in the poem [[page1959]]. Many scholars remain cautious, noting that the poem reflects the social world of the poet's own time more than that of the Bronze Age.

debates.title: Unity: the Doloneia and Book 24
text: An ancient note records that Book 10 was composed separately by Homer and inserted into the Iliad later, and many modern scholars regard it as non-Homeric because of its language, tone and self-containment [[kirk1985]]. Casey Dué and Mary Ebbott have defended it as an example of a traditional ambush theme in oral epic poetry, which a performance tradition would naturally include [[due2010]].

The ending of the poem has also been questioned by analysts, who saw Book 24 as a later addition. Most modern critics, however, regard Book 24 as essential to the poem's design, completing the story of Akhilleus' wrath and mirroring Book 1 [[macleod1982]] [[taplin1992]].

debates.title: The gods: serious or comic?
text: The Homeric gods quarrel, deceive, laugh and make love while men die. Since antiquity critics have been troubled by their apparent frivolity: Plato wanted Homer banned from his ideal state partly because of his depiction of the gods. Modern scholars have tried to understand the gods' role in the poem's meaning.

Jasper Griffin argued that the gods serve as a foil to mortal suffering: their ease and immortality make the seriousness of human life and death stand out [[griffin1980]]. Wolfgang Kullmann studied the relationship between gods and men across both epics [[kullmann1985]]. Others emphasise the gods' role as guardians of justice, oaths and suppliants.

debates.title: The heroic code and Akhilleus' refusal
text: Akhilleus' rejection of Agamemnon's gifts in Book 9 is central to interpreting the poem. Some critics see it as a challenge to the heroic code itself, an awareness that material rewards cannot compensate for the loss of life [[whitman1958]]. Others see it as a violation of community values, leading to the tragedy of Patroclus' death [[redfield1975]].

Adam Parry argued that Akhilleus has no language to express his disillusion except the heroic language, so that his speech seems contradictory [[parry1956]]. Seth Schein emphasised Akhilleus' tragic understanding of mortality [[schein1984]].

debates.title: Weil's 'poem of force' and war
text: Simone Weil's essay, written in 1939–40 and published in the Marseilles journal Cahiers du Sud in 1940–41 under the anagram 'Émile Novis', read the Iliad as a poem about force, the power that turns human beings into things, victims and victors alike [[weil1945]]. Written as France fell, the essay has shaped generations of readers who see the Iliad as the most clear-sighted of war poems, one that never mistakes force for virtue and extends the same bitterness to victors and vanquished.

Critics who resist Weil point out that the poem admires courage, skill and the beauty of armed men, and that its heroes find meaning, not only degradation, in battle; the Iliad mourns war without renouncing it. The psychiatrist Jonathan Shay compared Akhilleus to Vietnam veterans suffering from combat trauma, opening a new strand of interpretation [[shay1994]].

debates.title: The Shield of Akhilleus
text: The description of the Shield in Book 18 has generated much discussion. Is it a realistic description of a work of art, a cosmic image, or a symbol of the poem? Oliver Taplin argued that the shield shows the world in which the war is set, and that its scenes of peace give perspective on the violence of the poem [[taplin1980]].

Others read the shield as an image of the universe, or as a commentary on the poem's themes of justice, community and death. Its relation to Akhilleus, who carries it into his most violent fighting, remains a fruitful question [[edwards1987]].

quotes.quote: The wrath sing, goddess, of Peleus' son, Achilles, that destructive wrath which brought countless woes upon the Achaeans, and sent forth to Hades many valiant souls of heroes, and made them themselves spoil for dogs and every bird; thus the plan of Zeus came to fulfillment, from the time when first they parted in strife Atreus' son, king of men, and brilliant Achilles.
quotes.explanation: The proem announces the subject of the poem: not the whole Trojan War, but the wrath of Akhilleus and its consequences. The narrator invokes the goddess (the Muse), presents the cost of the wrath in terms of the dead left unburied, and places the events within the plan of Zeus. The opening also sets the poem's tragic tone: its subject is not victory but suffering.

quotes.quote: Even as are the generations of leaves, such are those also of men. As for the leaves, the wind scattereth some upon the earth, but the forest, as it bourgeons, putteth forth others when the season of spring is come; even so of men one generation springeth up and another passeth away.
quotes.explanation: Asked about his ancestry by Diomedes, Glaucus first reflects on the transience of human generations. The simile compares human beings to leaves, renewed each spring but individually brief. It places the heroic world within the cycle of nature and introduces a theme of mortality that the poem develops throughout.

quotes.quote: For my mother the goddess, silver-footed Thetis, telleth me that twofold fates are bearing me toward the doom of death: if I abide here and war about the city of the Trojans, then lost is my home-return, but my renown shall be imperishable; but if I return home to my dear native land, lost then is my glorious renown, yet shall my life long endure, neither shall the doom of death come soon upon me.
quotes.explanation: Akhilleus reveals the choice that defines him: glory in exchange for a short life, or a long life without fame. The opposition of kleos and nostos is the essence of the heroic condition. His decision to stay, later confirmed after Patroclus' death, makes him the tragic hero of the poem.

quotes.quote: Ah friend, if once escaped from this battle we were for ever to be ageless and immortal, neither should I fight myself amid the foremost, nor should I send thee into battle where men win glory; but now—for in any case fates of death beset us, fates past counting, which no mortal may escape or avoid—now let us go forward, whether we shall give glory to another, or another to us.
quotes.explanation: Sarpedon explains the heroic code to Glaucus: if men were immortal, there would be no need to fight. But since death is inevitable, they must seek glory. Mortality is the foundation of heroic action.

quotes.quote: Ah unhappy pair, wherefore gave we you to king Peleus, to a mortal, while ye are ageless and immortal? Was it that among wretched men ye too should have sorrows? For in sooth there is naught, I ween, more miserable than man among all things that breathe and move upon earth.
quotes.explanation: Zeus pities Akhilleus' immortal horses, which weep for Patroclus. His reflection on the misery of human life is one of the poem's most pessimistic statements, made all the more striking by being uttered by the king of the gods.

quotes.quote: Straightway may I die, seeing I was not to bear aid to my comrade at his slaying. Far, far from his own land hath he fallen, and had need of me to be a warder off of ruin.
quotes.explanation: Akhilleus' response to Thetis' warning that his death will follow Hector's. He accepts death as the price of avenging Patroclus, whom he failed to protect. The choice of Book 9 is now made definitively, out of grief rather than ambition.

quotes.quote: Nay, friend, do thou too die; why lamentest thou thus? Patroclus also died, who was better far than thou. And seest thou not what manner of man am I, how comely and how tall? A good man was my father, and a goddess the mother that bare me; yet over me too hang death and mighty fate.
quotes.explanation: Akhilleus' words to Lycaon combine cruelty with a strange solidarity. He kills a suppliant, but he also recognises that he himself is mortal. The passage anticipates the recognition between Akhilleus and Priam in Book 24.

quotes.quote: Nay, but not without a struggle let me die, neither ingloriously, but in the working of some great deed for the hearing of men that are yet to be.
quotes.explanation: Deceived by Athena, Hector realises that he is doomed. His response is to seek glory in death. The passage is the clearest example of how kleos functions as the answer to mortality.

quotes.quote: Lo, I am more piteous far than he, and have endured what no other mortal on the face of earth hath yet endured, to reach forth my hand to the face of him that hath slain my sons.
quotes.explanation: Priam's supplication of Akhilleus. He asks Akhilleus to remember his own father, and describes his act as one that no other mortal has endured. The gesture moves Akhilleus to tears and leads to the return of Hector's body.

quotes.quote: For two urns are set upon the floor of Zeus of gifts that he giveth, the one of ills, the other of blessings.
quotes.explanation: Akhilleus consoles Priam with a parable of the two jars from which Zeus distributes good and evil. All mortals receive a mixture of good and evil, or only evil. The speech expresses a view of human life as shared suffering.

questions.q: Why does the Iliad begin with the wrath of Akhilleus rather than the beginning of the Trojan War?
questions.hint: Consider how the narrow focus creates a tragic structure. Think about how the poem nonetheless includes the whole war through flashback, foreshadowing and set pieces like the Catalogue and the teichoskopia.

questions.q: Is Akhilleus right to reject Agamemnon's offer in Book 9?
questions.hint: Weigh Akhilleus' arguments about honour and mortality against the appeals of Phoenix and Ajax. Think about the consequences of his refusal and how the poem judges them.

questions.q: Compare Hector and Akhilleus as heroes.
questions.hint: Look at their motivations (shame, glory, family, friendship), their relationships with others, and their deaths. Consider why the poem ends with Hector's funeral.

questions.q: What role do the gods play in the Iliad? Are they serious or comic?
questions.hint: Examine scenes such as the quarrel on Olympus, the wounding of Aphrodite, the deception of Zeus, and the death of Sarpedon. Consider how the gods illuminate the human condition.

questions.q: How does the Iliad represent women?
questions.hint: Look at Helen, Andromache, Hecuba, Briseis and the goddesses. Consider their roles as prizes, mourners and voices of the costs of war.

questions.q: Is the Iliad a celebration of war or a criticism of it?
questions.hint: Consider Simone Weil's reading of the poem as a poem of force, the similes of peace, the Shield of Akhilleus, and the poem's admiration for heroic courage.

questions.q: What is the significance of the Shield of Akhilleus?
questions.hint: Describe the scenes on the shield and consider how they relate to the poem's themes. Think about why the shield is made at this point in the story.

questions.q: How does Book 24 resolve the poem?
questions.hint: Compare it with Book 1: supplication, ransom, quarrel and reconciliation. Consider what Akhilleus learns, and why the poem ends with a funeral.

questions.q: What does the Iliad suggest about friendship?
questions.hint: Focus on Akhilleus and Patroclus, but also consider Glaucus and Diomedes, Sarpedon and Glaucus, and the relationship between Akhilleus and Priam.

questions.q: How does oral composition shape the style of the Iliad?
questions.hint: Look at epithets, formulas, typical scenes and similes. Consider how repetition creates meaning and how the poet varies traditional material.
